relations.myth: The celestial helper descends to aid Asháninka fighters
relations.note: Amachénga and Itomi Pavá overlap as returning celestial-helper categories, though exact equivalence remains disputed.
Amachegua assist shamans in combating malevolent Kamári forces.
Good celestial spirits are classified as itome Pawa, children of Pava.
An Amachegua claimed Father Sun sent him to deliver political instructions.
Some accounts equate Tasórentsi with Amachegua; others make them the highest rank.
In the Awajún cycle, Ayaymama is Nántu's wife.
relations.source: Auju nantujai / La ayaymama y el luna

relations.myth: Ayaymama conceals ripe squash from Moon
relations.note: She eats ripe squash secretly and serves Nántu unripe squash.
relations.source: Auju nantujai / La ayaymama y el luna

relations.note: In the usual Asháninka genealogy, Avíreri is Kíri’s grandfather.

relations.myth: Avíreri and Kíri merge in the palm variant
relations.note: One Asháninka variant does not distinguish them and makes Avíreri the peach-palm.
Quërí is Mábireri’s young relative; the precise kin relationship varies.
Poporrona’ is explicitly Ayots’s son, whom he carries because he cannot walk.
Ayots names encountered beings in response to Poporrona’s questions, transforming them.
Avíreri carries Kíri, who prompts transformations, mourns him, and later becomes peach-palm.
Mábireri carries Quërí and transforms encountered people after the child questions him.

relations.myth: Ayots carries Poporrona' during his transforming journey
relations.note: Poporrona's repeated questions provoke Ayots into transforming encountered primordial people.

relations.myth: Poporrona' plans to repeat Ayots's cannibal flood
relations.note: Poporrona' inherits Ayots's transformative powers and plans to imitate his river-damming flood.
relations.source: Santos-Granero, Saint Christopher in the Amazon

relations.note: Avíreri carries Kíri, whose questions prompt him to transform encountered people.
Grieving for his grandfather, Kíri follows Avíreri but is overtaken and killed.

relations.myth: Mábireri and Quërí form the Nomatsigenga pair
relations.note: Quërí accompanies the elder transformer Mábireri, though accessible details remain incomplete.
Rojas identifies Wise’s character called Tasorentsi as Avíreri bearing the class-title.
Ayots, the gigantic malicious being, is expressly called Yato’ Yos’s son.
The bufeo’s blowhole is compared to Chullachaqui’s mismatched or animal foot.
relations.source: Las tres mitades de Ino Moxo

relations.note: Some Napo and Loreto accounts classify the bufeo as a water person.

relations.myth: The dolphin assumes human form to seek a lover
relations.note: Yacuruna may manifest as a dolphin disguised as a human lover or acquaintance.
relations.source: Regan, Hacia la tierra sin mal

relations.note: Modern Spanish-regional discourse compares Chullachaqui with deceptive kamari forest beings.
A children’s project makes Runamula and Chullachaqui the parents of Runachaqui.
Regionally treated as another name or locally equivalent forest being.
relations.source: Regan, Hacia la tierra sin mal

relations.note: A skeptic warned that the supposed Itomi Pavá might instead be a deceptive kamári.
relations.source: Brown and Fernández, War of Shadows

relations.note: Kashíri fathers the Sun, making Pavá’s children his indirect descendants.
Itomi Pavá literally denotes Pavá’s son or children and celestial emissaries.

relations.myth: Return of a son of the Sun
relations.note: Divine children and returning civilizing emissaries bear this relational title.
relations.source: Brown and Fernández, War of Shadows

relations.note: One consultant classified kamári as maninkari because both are invisible; others opposed the categories.
Benevolent invisible beings are structurally contrasted with harmful kamari.
Modern speakers may broadly classify Pishtaco as kamari despite important differences.
Some recent Christianized accounts say Tasorintsi created all beings, including kamari.
Modern regional discourse sometimes assimilates Tunche to kamori, Sashintsi, or whistling dead spirits.
Koriošpiri is called the father of the kamari or demons.
Korioshpiri governs Sharinkaueni as lord, ruler, or protector of its demons.
Koriošpiri rules the kamari or demons.
Kashiri periodically fights the Sun, causing eclipses.
Kashiri impregnates a woman who bears the solar being and dies.
They lived among humans and taught proper life before Pavá withdrew.
Tasorentsi co-creates Kashiri Ash and arranges his lunar marriage.
Kashíri, the Moon, is listed among the principal transforming beings called tasorentsi.
Maninkari identified as angels serve within Pavá’s heavenly court.
Some recent classifications place maninkari alongside or beneath tasorentsi.
Some traditions identify singular Tasorentsi with Pavá, the solar Father.
Some regional accounts call Tasorentsi a son, child, or emissary of Pavá.
Poporrona' is Yato' Yos's grandson through Ayots.
Aquatic Yacumama is Sachamama’s complementary water-serpent counterpart.
They emerge from Ukhu Pacha and connect the lower, middle, and upper worlds.

relations.myth: Joint passage through the three worlds
relations.note: They emerge underground, assume river and tree forms, then ascend as lightning and rainbow.

relations.myth: The water person appears as a great boa
relations.note: Yacuruna overlap or transform into great boas understood as water owners or deceased shamans.

relations.myth: Rival creation of beneficial and harmful beings
relations.note: Yosoper imitates Yato’ Yos, producing rival harmful creatures and demons.

relations.myth: Creation of the intermediate human world
relations.note: Yosoper gives or lends earth that Yato’ Yos uses for another world.
The bad brother offers saliva; Yato’ Yos refuses to avoid his control.
Yosoper is Yato’ Yos’s elder or classificatory brother and creative antagonist.

relations.myth: Appropriation of the first new earth
relations.note: Yosoper appropriates the first lower earth created by Yato’ Yos.

Anitetepue.myth: Anitetepue kills the abandoned children's mother
Anitetepue.note: After Anitetepue kills their mother, Ayaymama imitates the children's lament.

Antichrist.note: One modern Asháninka interview explicitly identifies Korioshpiri as the Antichrist.

Armadillo.note: Armadillo is Ayots or Avíreri’s brother-in-law through his unnamed sister.

Armadillo.myth: Armadillo seals Ayots in an underground house
Armadillo.note: After Ayots transforms his children, Armadillo traps and permanently confines him underground.

Armadillo.myth: Avíreri’s fall through the dancing-ground trap
Armadillo.note: After falling into the trap, Avíreri transforms his frightened brother-in-law into armadillo.

Aroshi.note: Kashiri tries to swallow Aroshi, who escapes after tearing his garment.
In a competing version Kashiri devours Aroshi, whose remains mark the full moon.

Asha.note: Asha is a lunar-phase child of the couple created by Tasorentsi.

Ashe.note: Kashiri Ash and Kashiri Aah produce Ashe, representing waxing quarter.
Ashe is a lunar-phase child of the couple created by Tasorentsi.

Ashinsateri.note: Ashinsateri is documented as a kamari-like white mist causing madness and death.

Asho.note: Kashiri Ash and Kashiri Aah produce Asho, representing waning quarter.
Asho is a lunar-phase child of the couple created by Tasorentsi.

Carlos Fermín Fitzcarrald.myth: White stranger claims Father Sun sent him
Carlos Fermín Fitzcarrald.note: Reyna retrospectively identified the 1888 Amachengua claimant with Fitzcarrald; the equation remains unproven.
Carlos Fermín Fitzcarrald.source: Reyna, Fitzcarraldo, el rey del caucho

Christian Devil.note: Missionaries classified indigenous aquatic beings as devils within Christian demonology.

Christian God.note: Converted discourse renders benevolent spirits as children of the Christian God.
Evangelization applied Pavá terminology to the true Christian Father above older divinities.

Christian demons.note: Missionary and bilingual discourse translates kamari as Christian demons.

Ciraráto.note: The bird-being Ciraráto prevents Avíreri completing a dam intended to destroy the Asháninka.

Conkíri.note: Conkíri's theft prompts Aroshi's expedition to Kashiri, though they may never meet.

Etsa.myth: Etsa transforms fallen Ayaymama into a bird
Etsa.note: Etsa makes Ayaymama a lamenting bird and her spilled squash clay.
Etsa.source: Auju nantujai / La ayaymama y el luna

Ferdinand A. Stahl.myth: Adventist preaching prompts expectations of immediate celestial renewal
Ferdinand A. Stahl.note: Some followers identified Stahl or his mission station with the expected divine agent.
Ferdinand A. Stahl.source: Bodley materials summarized by Brown and Fernández

God the Father.note: Christianized versions identify Kashiri with the father in a Father–Mary–Jesus triad.

Guillermo Lobatón.myth: Ernesto recognizes the MIR commander as Son of the Sun
Guillermo Lobatón.note: Shaman Ernesto Andrés identified Lobatón as Itomi Pavá, mobilizing supporters before catastrophic disconfirmation.
Guillermo Lobatón.source: Brown and Fernández, War of Shadows

Iguiane.note: Pareni and Kinteroni retaliate after Iguiane transforms her sons and daughters into animals.

Inca.myth: The killed Inca survives and will return
Inca.note: Some Asháninka narratives explicitly identify the killed and returning Inca as Itomi Pavá.

Inka.myth: The living severed head of Inka
Inka.note: Post-contact myths call Inka a son of Pavá who provides manufactured wealth.
Inka.source: Brown and Fernández, War of Shadows

Inka.note: Inka is included among the principal tasorentsi in Asháninka cosmology.

Inkanítari.note: The rain deity Inkanítari is listed among the principal tasorentsi.

Irampavanto.note: Irampavanto is a kamari form that seduces victims before beating them to death.

Jesus.note: Christianized versions identify Kashiri's solar son with Jesus.
Maninkari identified as angels serve around the Lamb in the heavenly court.

Jesus Christ.note: Sala polemically declared Jesus the only true Amachegua.

Jesus Christ.myth: Missionary identification of the returning celestial savior
Jesus Christ.note: Missionaries equated the true Amachegua or returning Son of Pavá with Christ.
Jesus Christ.source: Sala diary; Stahl and Bodley materials

Juan Santos Atahualpa.note: Later accounts identified the reported 1888 Amachegua as Juan Santos reincarnated.

Juan Santos Atahualpa.myth: The rebel survives or reincarnates as returning savior
Juan Santos Atahualpa.note: Later traditions identify Juan Santos as a manifestation or predecessor of Itomi Pavá.
Juan Santos Atahualpa.source: Brown and Fernández, War of Shadows

Kaganiri.note: Kaganiri is a nearly invisible, silent wind that freezes its victim.

Kashiri Aah.note: Male Kashiri Ash marries female Kashiri Aah in Jananeria.
Tasorentsi and Oitasatsi create the female lunar being and arrange her marriage.
Tasorentsi and Oitasatsi marry her to the male lunar being.

Kashiri Ash.note: Tasorentsi and Oitasatsi create the male lunar being and arrange his marriage.
Tasorentsi and Oitasatsi marry him to the female lunar being.

Katsivoreri.note: Katsivoreri is a flying luminous kamari form associated with lethal sexual assault.

Katzereri.note: Katzereri are bright-eyed spirits carried by peyari, together forming a double demon.

Kentíparo.myth: Flying beings raise the dangerous Sun
Kentíparo.note: Kentíparo wraps Pavá in cushmas and carries him upward.

Kientibakori.note: A modern registry claims Kientibakori created kamari by conflating Matsigenka and Asháninka traditions.
Secondary accounts report Tasorentsi descending into Kientibakori’s realm for a duel.

Kinteroni.note: The primordial giant armadillo becomes Pareni’s final husband and father of many children.
Pareni and Kinteroni act together against those responsible for transforming their children.

Kitamari.note: Kitamari is a post-contact spirit appearing as a white donkey.

K’uychi.note: Upon reaching Hanan Pacha, Sachamama is identified with the rainbow.

Madre del Agua.note: Regan places the Mother of the Water within the broader Yacuruna transformational class.
Madre del Agua.source: Regan, Hacia la tierra sin mal

Mankoite.note: Mankoite is classified as a powerful kamari, sometimes nearly tasorentsi in power.

Moon-man.myth: Moon-man sleeps incestuously with his sister
Moon-man.note: The woman who becomes Ayaymama is Moon-man's sister and sexual partner.

Moon-man.myth: Moon-man ascends and the woman becomes Ayaymama
Moon-man.note: She marks his face with huito; after his ascent, she becomes Ayaymama.

Nantatziri.note: Some communities may classify these dwarf-like animal owners as kamari.

Neorónke.note: Neorónke fixes a vine to heaven, enabling Pavá’s ascent.

Oitasatsi.note: Oitasatsi creates the male lunar being Kashiri Ash.
They jointly create the lunar couple, convene celestial beings, and officiate their marriage.

Pachakamui.note: Pareni traps or casts Pachakamui into a chasm after Iguiane transforms her children.

Pachakamáite.note: Some traditions call the culture hero Pachakamáite a son of the Sun.

Pachákama.myth: Avíreri reaches Otsitiríko at River’s End
Pachákama.note: Pachákama prevents Avíreri’s return, keeping him bound by a strangler vine.

Pachákama.myth: Avíreri supports the earth at River’s End
Pachákama.note: At Pachákama’s request, Avíreri remains at Otsitiríko helping support the earth.
Some Matsigenka usage reportedly treats Pachákama and the Avíreri-equivalent interchangeably.
Pachákama belongs to the powerful transforming beings collectively called tasorentsi.

Pavá’s daughters.myth: Daughters ascend and leave their clothing
Pavá’s daughters.note: Pavá fathers daughters whose discarded clothing becomes seasonal trees and flowers.

Pawa.note: Some recent Christianized accounts say Pawa created all beings, including kamari.
Amônia tradition makes the eternally existing Pawa creator of Kashiri.

Pichokiti.note: The bird who impregnates the woman assumes or reveals Kashiri's identity.

Plant ánimas or madres.note: Shapshico can situationally name a medicinal plant’s animate owner, guardian, or teacher.

Purahua.myth: Karuara resist Purahua's destructive riverbank erosion
Purahua.note: Karuara oppose Purahua and protect land threatened by the great water-serpent.

Runachaqui.note: A children’s cultural project names Runamula as Runachaqui’s mother.

Sacaramentaro.myth: Divine warrior preserving the Juan Santos tradition
Sacaramentaro.note: Scholarly reconstruction tentatively connects Sacaramentaro through Juan Santos with Itomi Pavá.

Sacharuna.note: Regan presents Sacharuna as an equivalent forest-person or forest-owner category.
Sacharuna.source: Regan, Hacia la tierra sin mal

Sacramentaro.note: This anti-colonial transformer is called a Pavá or god, not securely the Sun.

Saint Christopher.note: Santos-Granero proposes Ayots and Avíreri as an inverted Indigenous transformation of Saint Christopher.
Saint Christopher.source: Santos-Granero, Saint Christopher in the Amazon

Santa María.note: The woman impregnated by Kashiri is identified as Santa María.

Santosaprecoya.note: Santosaprecoya is called Yato’ Yos’s daughter.
After producing medicinal plants from milk, she returns to Yato’ Yos in heaven.

Sashintsi.note: Sashintsi is a skeletal kamari form that breaks, restores, and sends victims home to die.

Shiiro.note: Shiiro becomes Pareni’s husband and feeds by sucking her sweat.
Pareni transforms the sweat-drinking Shiiro into a sweat bee.

Shitati.note: Shitati becomes Pareni’s dependent husband, refusing ordinary food while demanding sustenance.
Pareni makes Shitati a dung beetle after he consumes her excrement.

Sirena.note: Sirens are classified as Yacuruna or as transformations within the same aquatic complex.
Sirena.source: Regan, Hacia la tierra sin mal

The Maligno.myth: The Maligno hunts the good Tunche
The Maligno.note: A condemned Maligno pursues the less dangerous Tunche to transfer guilt.
Some tellings merge the Tunche and Maligno into one being.

Tsonkiri.note: Tsonkiri becomes Pareni’s husband and receives fish secretly drawn from her body.
After Tsonkiri spies on her fish source, Pareni makes him a flower-feeding hummingbird.

Uiara.note: The aquatic lover and master is associated or fused with the boto.

Werner Bulner.myth: Followers journey to Bulner’s Río Ene mission
Werner Bulner.note: Some Asháninka and Nomatsiguenga hailed Bulner as Itomi Pavá, then repudiated the identification.

Yashingo.note: Loreto and Ucayali sources use these names for comparable or identical forest devils.

Yato’ Yos.note: Ayots is one of the supreme creator Yato’ Yos’s sons.
Yosoper is Yato’ Yos’s classificatory brother or brother by alliance.

Yato’ Yos.myth: Appropriation of the first flat earth
Yato’ Yos.note: Jealous Yosoper takes possession of the flat earth created by Yato’ Yos.
Yosoper imitates Yato’ Yos’s clay human by making ten similar beings.
Yosoper copies each species Yato’ Yos creates, producing numerous harmful counterparts.

Yompor Ror.note: Some summaries treat Ror as Yato’ Yos’s son or descendant.
Yato’ Yos sends the flower that miraculously impregnates Ror’s mother.

Yompor Rret.note: Yato’ Yos appoints Rret to illuminate creation, but Rret becomes destructive.

Yompor Santo.note: Later tradition presents Yompor Santo as Yato’ Yos’s son or divine emissary.
Yato’ Yos sends his emissary to rescue the Yanesha and restore immortality.

angels.note: Christianized speakers and Bible translators identify maninkari with biblical angels.

demons.note: Yosoper creates ten humanlike beings that Yato’ Yos curses into demons.

firmament Sun.note: Kashiri fathers a firmament Sun that illuminates the stars.

jo’.note: Yato’ Yos transforms some of Yosoper’s imitative persons into demonic beings.

oneñet.note: Yato’ Yos transforms some of Yosoper’s imitative persons into demonic beings.

peyari.note: Contemporary discourse increasingly merges transformed or wandering dead called peyari with kamari.

underworld Sun.note: Matsigenka accounts make an underworld Sun one of Kashiri's sons.

yellow-headed vulture.myth: Vulture causes the transformed palm's thorns
yellow-headed vulture.note: After Poporrona' becomes a palm, the vulture's prick and response produce trunk thorns.

Ñeñephnor Partsophnor Yarrona’.note: She is the sister who supplies milk for Yato’ Yos’s creation.

Ñeñephnor Partsophnor Yarrona’.myth: Creation of earth from a milk-drop
Ñeñephnor Partsophnor Yarrona’.note: She expresses the milk-drop from which Yato’ Yos forms the earth.
